questions.problem:
Suppose we have a random sample of size $n=66$ from a population where $42%$ of the population has a particular characteristic. Let the random variable ${X}_{i}$ be equal to

$$
{X}_{i}=\{\begin{aligned}1,\,i\text{th member of the sample has the characteristic} \\ 0,\,\text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$

where $i=1,…,66.$ Find an approximate sampling distribution of the statistic $X={\sum }_{i=1}^{66}{X}_{i}.$

*Hint: You may assume that the population size is significantly larger than the sample size.*
questions.worked_solution:
Suppose we have a random sample of size $n$ from a population of size $N,$ and we define the sequence of random variables ${X}_{i}$ as follows:

$$
{X}_{i}=\{\begin{aligned}1,\,i\text{th member of the sample has the characteristic} \\ 0,\,\text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, provided that $N≫n,$ the random variables ${X}_{i}$ can be considered independent and identically distributed. Under this assumption, we have

$$
{X}_{i}∼\text{Bernoulli}(p)\,1\le i\le n
$$

where $p$ is the proportion of the population that has the characteristic.

Therefore, the random variable $X,$ defined as 

$$
X={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{X}_{i}
$$

can be approximated as a binomial random variable $X≈B(n,p).$ 

In our case, we're told that the population size is significantly larger than the sample size. Moreover, we have 

$$
p=42%=0.42,\,n=66.
$$

Therefore,

$$
X≈B(66,0.42).
$$

questions.problem:
Suppose we have a random sample of size $n=140$ from a population where $60%$ of the population has a particular characteristic. Let the random variable ${X}_{i}$ be equal to

$$
{X}_{i}=\{\begin{aligned}1,\,i\text{th member of the sample has the characteristic} \\ 0,\,\text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$

where $i=1,…,140.$ If the statistic $X$ is defined as

$$
X={\sum }_{i=1}^{140}{X}_{i}
$$

find approximate values of $\text{E}[X]$ and $\text{Var}[X].$

*Hint: You may assume that the population size is significantly larger than the sample size.*
questions.worked_solution:
Suppose we have a random sample of size $n$ from a population of size $N,$ and we define the sequence of random variables ${X}_{i}$ as follows:

$$
{X}_{i}=\{\begin{aligned}1,\,i\text{th member of the sample has the characteristic} \\ 0,\,\text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, provided that $N≫n,$ the random variables ${X}_{i}$ can be considered independent and identically distributed. Under this assumption, we have

$$
{X}_{i}∼\text{Bernoulli}(p)\,1\le i\le n
$$

where $p$ is the proportion of the population that has the characteristic.

Therefore, the random variable $X,$ defined as 

$$
X={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{X}_{i}
$$

can be approximated as a binomial random variable $X≈B(n,p),$ where

$$
\text{E}[X]=np,\,\text{Var}[X]=np(1-p).
$$

In our case, we're told that the population size is significantly larger than the sample size. Moreover, we have 

$$
p=60%=0.6,\,n=140.
$$

Therefore,

$$
X≈B(140,0.6)
$$

and we have the following results for the mean and variance:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X] & =np \\  & =140\cdot 0.6 \\  & =84 \\ \text{Var}[X] & =np(1-p) \\  & =140\cdot 0.6\cdot (1-0.6) \\  & =33.6\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Suppose that $60%$ of the child population enrolled in a baseball academy is right-handed. A random sample of $n=20$ children is taken from the population and asked about their dominant hand.

What is the mean and variance of $\overset{^}{\,p},$ the proportion of right-handed children in the sample? 

*Hint: You may assume that the population size is significantly larger than the sample size.*
questions.worked_solution:
Suppose we have a random sample of size $n$ from a population of size $N,$ and we define the sequence of random variables ${X}_{i}$ as follows:

$$
{X}_{i}=\{\begin{aligned}1,\,i\text{th member of the sample has the characteristic}, \\ 0,\,\text{otherwise}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, provided that $N≫n,$ we have that

$$
X={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{X}_{i}≈B(n,p)
$$

where $p$ is the proportion of the population that have the characteristic, and 

$$
\text{E}[X]=np,\,\text{Var}[X]=np(1-p).
$$

The sample proportion $\overset{^}{\,p}$ is given by

$$
\overset{^}{\,p}=\overset{―}{X}=\frac{X}{n}.
$$

Using the properties of expectation and variance, it is straightforward to show that

$$
\text{E}[\overset{^}{\,p}]=p,\,\text{Var}[\overset{^}{\,p}]=\frac{p(1-p)}{n}.
$$

In our case, we have $p=60%=0.6,$ and $n=20.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[\overset{^}{\,p}] & =60%=0.6, \\ \text{Var}[\overset{^}{\,p}] & =\frac{0.6(1-0.6)}{20} \\  & =0.012.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the properties of expectation and variance, it is straightforward to show that

$$
\text{E}[\overset{^}{\,p}]=p,\,\text{Var}[\overset{^}{\,p}]=\frac{p(1-p)}{n}.

questions.problem:
It is known that  $5%$ of the researchers in a particular university work in neurobiology. A random sample of $n=15$ researchers is taken from the population and asked about their work area.

What is the mean and variance of $\overset{^}{\,p},$ the proportion of researchers in the sample working in neurobiology? Round your answers to $4$ decimal places where appropriate.

*Hint: You may assume that the population size is significantly larger than the sample size.*
questions.worked_solution:
Suppose we have a random sample of size $n$ from a population of size $N,$ and we define the sequence of random variables ${X}_{i}$ as follows:

$$
{X}_{i}=\{\begin{aligned}1,\,i\text{th member of the sample has the characteristic}, \\ 0,\,\text{otherwise}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, provided that $N≫n,$ we have that

$$
X={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{X}_{i}≈B(n,p)
$$

where $p$ is the proportion of the population that have the characteristic, and 

$$
\text{E}[X]=np,\,\text{Var}[X]=np(1-p).
$$

The sample proportion $\overset{^}{\,p}$ is given by

$$
\overset{^}{\,p}=\overset{―}{X}=\frac{X}{n}.
$$

Using the properties of expectation and variance, it is straightforward to show that

$$
\text{E}[\overset{^}{\,p}]=p,\,\text{Var}[\overset{^}{\,p}]=\frac{p(1-p)}{n}.
$$

In our case, we have $p=5%=0.05,$ and $n=15.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[\overset{^}{\,p}] & =5%=0.05, \\ \text{Var}[\overset{^}{\,p}] & =\frac{0.05(1-0.05)}{15} \\  & ≈0.0032\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $4$ decimal places.
